content.definition: The lens nucleus is the central compacted mass formed by the lens fibres laid down in utero and in early postnatal life, enclosed by the younger shells of the cortex. It is demarcated from the cortex by the junction of fetal and postnatal fibres — because the lens is about 6.5 mm wide at birth, this junction marks the width of the postnatal nucleus — and within it the embryonic, fetal and adult nuclei are distinguished from one another by their successive suture patterns, the lines along which the tips of the fibres of each generation meet. The sutures become increasingly complex as the lens grows: the fetal nucleus carries an anterior erect Y and a posterior inverted Y, further growth adds symmetrical branching that ultimately forms the 9-point star of the mature cortex, and senescent lenses show further irregular sub-branching. The nucleus differs optically from the cortex in having a higher refractive index, the refractive index changing in graded fashion from cortex to nucleus in correlation with protein content — an arrangement that accounts for the overall refractive power of the lens and its relative freedom from chromatic aberration (Phillipson 1969).
content.location: The nucleus occupies the central core of the lens, deep to the cortex, extending pole to pole and across the equator. Its outer boundary is arbitrary but taken at the junction of fetal and postnatal fibres, so that in the adult the nucleus comprises the embryonic and fetal nuclei plus the adult nucleus formed by fibres added after birth; the cortical shells lie outside it. The older the fibre generation, the deeper it lies and the more it is affected by the central compaction that reduces nuclear width during the first two decades of postnatal life, while the cortical width increases (Forbes et al. 1992).
layers: Embryonic nucleus: the innermost mass formed by the primary lens fibres that elongated from the posterior wall of the lens vesicle during the 6th-7th week of intrauterine life (18 mm embryo); enclosed by the anterior erect and posterior inverted Y-sutures of the fetal nucleus

Fetal nucleus: the fibres of the secondary generations laid down in utero; its Y-suture branches arise over a span of 60 longitudinal degrees of the equator and insert into suture branches measuring 30 longitudinal degrees, the fibres being much wider at the equator than at the sutures and the curvature more pronounced because there are only six branches

Adult (postnatal) nucleus: fibres added after birth until about the end of the second decade; its suture system branches symmetrically into the 9-point star of the mature cortex, in which eight distinct arms turn precisely in the meridional plane at an angle of 20 degrees, half terminating at the anterior pole and half at the posterior pole

Zones of optical discontinuity (slit-lamp zones): a clear cortical zone (C1-alpha) develops postnatally; the ageing C1-beta fibres generate proto-C2,3,4; at roughly 7 years a zone of increased scattering, C3, appears and increases in scattering throughout life, separating a deeper perinuclear C4 from a more superficial C2; each successive star position is generated over about 15 years (Fig 12.37)
content.blood_supply: The nucleus is avascular and deeply placed, and its metabolic activity at the centre of the lens is negligible: its proteins do not turn over significantly (Harding and Dilley 1976) and are therefore extremely long-lived and vulnerable to oxidative and other influences. Its ionic environment is controlled remotely by the pump-leak system (Kinsey and Reddy 1965): the epithelium and possibly some superficial cortical fibres serve as the major pump system of the lens, transporting sodium forwards and outwards by the activity of Na+/K+-activated ATPase (there is also a calcium-activated pump, and potassium moves into the lens anteriorly), while at the posterior aspect of the lens there is passive diffusion of sodium inwards and potassium outwards. Equilibration between individual fibres and the epithelium is facilitated by the gap junctions (Fig 12.38). The substrates arrive from the aqueous, whose glucose content is similar to that of plasma (about 100 mg%) and whose oxygen tension is about 60 mmHg (Cole 1974); energy is chiefly glycolytic, the small aerobic fraction (about 3% of glucose, up to 20% of energy needs; van Heyningen 1969) being confined to the epithelium and most superficial cortical fibres and therefore not available to the nucleus itself.
content.histology_summary: Growth of the nucleus follows a precise timetable. From the 6th-7th week of intrauterine life (18 mm embryo) the primary fibres elongate in the anteroposterior direction; during the 18-24 mm stage the lens is approximately spherical; with the appearance of the secondary fibres at the 26 mm stage the lens becomes wider in its equatorial diameter; the zonule appears later, at the 65 mm stage of fetal life, and plays no role in this initial widening. At birth the lens is almost spherical but wider in the equatorial plane, and the fetal lens grows in mass through uterine life (Ehlers, Mathiessen and Anderson 1968). In the first two decades after birth, sagittal expansion ceases while growth continues in the equatorial plane; this period is dominated by a vigorous compaction of the nucleus — the sagittal width remains relatively stationary while the nuclear width decreases and the combined cortical width increases (Forbes et al. 1992, Fig 12.36) — and compaction is probably the most potent factor determining the plateau of sagittal growth, while rising zonular tension with transverse growth of the globe contributes to the preferential equatorial enlargement. From about the age of 20 years, nuclear compaction completed, sagittal growth resumes and equatorial growth becomes negligible; throughout adult life the lens adds about 29 um per year to its sagittal thickness (Nielsen 1982; Brown 1973), the total sagittal width following y = 3.6234 + 1.1538e-2x + 1.8593e-4x^2 (R = 0.875) over the whole lifespan (Forbes et al. 1992). The specific gravity of the lens remains more or less constant although the lens expands in all dimensions, but the nuclear density significantly increases in the ageing eye (Bours and Fodisch 1986; Bours et al. 1987): direct measurement suggested a small dehydration of the nucleus with age, whereas Siebinga et al. (1991), using Raman spectroscopy, found hydration to increase with age. The suture geometry is exact: in the adult 9-point star each of the eight distinct arms turns precisely in the meridional plane at 20 degrees, fibres ending slightly anteriorly (10 degrees latitude) on one side and posteriorly on the other; because the equatorial circumference of the fibres is shorter than the length of the sutures into which they insert, the fibre tips are expanded as well as curved (in a 4-star suture, fibres occupying 20 longitudinal degrees of the equator insert over more than 75 degrees at the suture). Fibre length varies only slightly with meridian, so the overlap within successive growth shells produces ordered meridional columns (Rabl 1903); in the postnatal lens, where fibre length is not a function of radial location, the sutures of successive shells do not lie in register but are offset, forming the symmetrical crystalline latticework of the star sutures (Fig 12.29). In the fetal nuclei there is a superimposition of the suture zones, visible on biomicroscopy, although the continuity of the suture plane is more difficult to see with the slit-lamp. A modern synthesis by Augusteyn (2010) reinterprets these zones: human lens growth is biphasic - asymptotic before birth and essentially linear thereafter - so that the nuclear core of fixed dimensions (corresponding to the combined slit-lamp nuclear zones) is complete within about three months of birth and all later growth adds cortex; on this evidence Augusteyn argues that the terms foetal, juvenile and adult nucleus are misleading and should be abandoned in favour of a prenatal core and a postnatal cortex. MRI measurement of the gradient refractive index (Jones, Atchison and Pope 2005) supplies the modern quantitative framework for the optical discontinuities seen at the slit-lamp.
content.clinical_importance: The optical qualities of the lens depend directly on nuclear structure: the multilayered fibre system, with nuclei displaced to the bow or absent from deeper fibres, minimizes fluctuations in back-scattering, and the graded refractive index from cortex to nucleus accounts for the overall refractive power and the relative freedom from chromatic aberration (Phillipson 1969). At birth the lens is perfectly transparent; with growth there is an increasing yellowing of the nucleus due probably to absorption of ultraviolet light (mainly 315-400 nm) of sunlight by chromophores, producing visible and fluorescent pigments that may serve to screen the retina from damaging short-wave blue light (Sliney and Wolbarsht 1980). Cortical pigments render the perinuclear cortex autofluorescent in blue exciting light, while pigments accumulating in the nucleus may in some individuals produce the brunescent colour of senile nuclear cataract. In the ageing nucleus, and particularly in nuclear cataract, an increasing quantity of insoluble protein is found, due to cross-linked and macromolecular aggregates of crystallins: because central metabolic activity is negligible and proteins do not turn over, they are extremely long-lived and vulnerable to oxidative unfolding that exposes sulphydryl groups, which engage in disulphide bonding with further crosslinking and conformational change. The opacity of cataract is due to zones of increased scattering within the lens substance — breakdown of fibre regularity, products of membrane degradation, and scattering by macromolecular aggregates — while swelling and fibre disorganization follow disturbances of ion and water regulation (Harding 1991; Brown and Bron 1996). Clinically, the suture planes are sites of increased spherical aberration (Kuszak, Sivak and Weeheim 1991a), the superimposed suture zones of the fetal nucleus and the successive zones of discontinuity allow the lens to be aged and opacities localized to embryonic, fetal, infantile or adult tissue at the slit-lamp, and the compaction of central fibres makes a traumatic opacity recede from the surface at approximately twice the speed at which the lens grows, allowing contusion opacities to be dated (Brown et al. 1988). Mechanical testing has quantified nuclear hardening: Heys, Cram and Truscott (2004) measured a massive age-related increase in nuclear stiffness - more than a thousand-fold between roughly 14 and 65 years of age - and this hardening of the nucleus, rather than failure of the ciliary muscle, is now widely held to be the principal mechanical basis of presbyopia.
